records.our_prose: Chives are one of the easiest and hardiest herbs you can grow. They are a perennial in the onion family, so you plant them once and they come back every year on their own. The plant dies back over winter, then sends up fresh, thin, grassy green leaves very early in spring, and it carries pretty pink-purple flowers in early summer that you can eat too. Chives like full sun to a little shade, decent soil, and regular water, but they forgive a lot. The clump gets bigger each year, so dig it up and split it every few years. They have a mild oniony taste and hardly any pests. There is also a relative called garlic chives, with flat leaves and a mild garlic flavor.

records.our_prose: Chives (Allium schoenoprasum) are a hardy, clump-forming perennial in the onion family (Amaryllidaceae), grown for their slender, hollow, grass-like leaves and their edible pink to pale purple pom-pom flowers. Unlike the annual and biennial kitchen herbs, chives are planted once and come back on their own year after year: the clump dies back to the ground over winter, rests dormant, and pushes up fresh green blades as one of the very first herbs of spring. They are among the hardiest herbs grown, reliable to roughly USDA zone 3, and among the easiest, with a mild onion flavor and few real pests. Give them full sun to light shade, average to rich well-drained soil, and steady moisture, though an established clump tolerates short dry spells. The clumps slowly widen from year to year and are best lifted and divided every 2 to 3 years to keep them vigorous. Chives are cool-preferring: in cold regions they run right through the northern summer, while in the hot South and desert they are a cool-season herb that slows or rests in the worst summer heat and revives as it cools. A close relative, garlic chives (Allium tuberosum), is a distinct species with flat leaves, a mild garlic flavor, and white late-summer flowers.

records.our_prose: The Las Vegas Valley grows chives as a hardy perennial planted once, in spring around the last frost, and cut repeatedly for years; the UNLV Master Gardener chart carries no chives-specific row, so this cell is modeled from the crop's own cool-preferring, cold-hardy perennial envelope and the University of Nevada, Reno Extension's home-vegetable framework (Fact Sheet FS-02-61). Once daytime highs push past the region's roughly 90°F growth ceiling from June into September, the clump slows, the leaves scorch, and cutting pauses; it resumes as the weather cools and the same clump is cut again through fall, then goes dormant over the mild winter. Divide the clump every 2 to 3 years to keep it vigorous. Zone 8's cooler pockets establish a little later in spring; zone 10 at Laughlin establishes earliest and its milder winter lets the fall cutting run a little longer.

records.our_prose: Chives tolerate a wide range of soils but grow best in a well-drained loam rich in organic matter, kept evenly moist. The University of Minnesota recommends well-drained soil rich in organic matter, and Michigan State notes chives grow best in soils high in organic matter while adapting to most soil types. Work compost into the bed before planting to feed a clump you cut from for years, and site it where water does not stand, since a waterlogged crown, especially over winter, invites rot on this otherwise trouble-free perennial.

records.our_prose: Chives are easiest to establish from a division or a nursery clump, which gives a cuttable plant in weeks, but they also grow readily from seed. The seed is slow, germinating over about 2 to 3 weeks (up to 4 to 6 in cool soil), so start it indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost, sowing a pinch of about 8 to 10 seeds per cell and growing them on as an undivided clump that transplants out whole after hardening off, with no thinning (RHS), or direct-sow once the soil warms. Plant outdoors in spring after hard-frost danger passes in cold regions, or in fall through late winter in mild and hot regions. Set clumps 8 to 12 inches apart; they widen over the years and are the easiest herb to propagate by simply lifting and splitting an established clump.

records.our_prose: Chives come in two distinct plants. Common chives (Allium schoenoprasum) are the familiar fine, hollow-leaved clump with pink-purple spring flowers and a mild onion taste; named selections differ mostly in leaf fineness and vigor, from the slender Fine Leaf and Grolau strains favored for pots and forcing, to the thick, easy-cutting Staro, to taller showy-flowered Forescate. Garlic chives (Allium tuberosum) are a separate species with flat leaves, a garlic flavor, and white late-summer flowers; they are tougher in heat and drought but self-sow aggressively. All are grown much the same way, so choice comes down to flavor (onion versus garlic), leaf form, and how much you value the flowers, while any chive self-seeds if you let the blooms set seed.
